results.finding: Patients with behavioural-variant frontal-network neurodegeneration often demonstrate financial and medical decision-making capacity impairment early in the disease course due to orbitofrontal dysfunction; legal instruments such as durable power of attorney and guardianship are described as appropriate clinical management considerations in the published literature
results.title: Decision-making capacity in frontal-network neurodegenerative syndromes

output.summary: Frontal-predominant neurodegeneration with orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal dysfunction causes early impairment in financial and medical decision-making capacity. Published literature documents that capacity impairment frequently precedes formal diagnosis and may manifest as reckless financial transactions, ethical violations, and impulsive decision-making. Legal planning instruments (durable power of attorney, healthcare proxy) are described in the literature as appropriate early interventions when capacity is impaired. Guardianship may be required when capacity for autonomous decision-making is lost.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: As an attorney, immediately address professional capacity (continuing client representation, fiduciary duties) and notify employer/state bar where required.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

clinical_assessment.impression: 3 of the six Rascovsky behavioural features are documented, against the three required for possible behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia, alongside a dysexecutive bedside profile. The diagnosis is behavioural and is made on this assessment; imaging supports it and does not substitute for it. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively spared, which is the discriminator against Alzheimer's disease and the reason a screening total alone understates the syndrome.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. P. is a 56-year-old attorney referred by his wife for progressive personality changes over 2 years. A previously respected litigator known for his meticulous preparation and professional demeanor, his behavior changed markedly 2 years ago. He began making inappropriate remarks to opposing counsel and judges in court. He was reprimanded by the state bar for sharing client confidences at a cocktail party. He made sexually inappropriate comments to a paralegal and was asked to resign. At home, he has become impulsive, making major financial decisions without consultation, has started collecting dozens of identical items (has purchased 40 identical blue pens online), and eats continuously. He cannot stop watching the same 3 movies on repeat. He shows no concern about the loss of his career. Wife notes he seems emotionally flat when with grandchildren but was previously extremely close with them. No family history of dementia.
